title: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit
description: The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues duri
body: The chief executive of the company that runs the Eiffel Tower will step down after a backlash over female staff being replaced by male colleagues during a visit by a Hindu religious group.Patrick Branco Ruivo, who has been director general of the Paris landmark since 2018, will leave his job at the end of the year, the company SETE said in a statement.It said an internal investigation found that "operational flaws and shortcomings" in organising the visit led to the "unacceptable" removal of female staff.They were replaced by male colleagues as a delegation of around 100 people linked to the Bochasanwasi Akshar Purushottam Swaminarayan Sanstha (BAPS) group visited the Eiffel Tower earlier this month.BAPS - a movement whose beliefs originate in the 18th Century - strictly separates men and women, including in temple activities and building entrances.At the time, SETE said the Hindu delegation had requested that the visit be organised so as to limit "interactions with women" and said that "these conditions should not have been accepted".A staff union representative said "women were asked to leave their places of work" and felt "humiliated". Staff at the monument said female employees were also "instructed not to go through or cross certain areas while the delegation was present".The visit led to the closure of the tower as staff went on strike to show their outrage and politicians condemned the incident.Yaël Braun-Pivet, the president of France's National Assembly, said after the visit: "I refuse to allow women to be compelled to step aside in order to meet the demands of foreign visitors."The Socialist mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Gregoire, called it an "absurd, unjust and unacceptable decision" and ordered two separate investigations.SETE chair Ariel Weil said on Tuesday that he had requested measures and training programmes promoting gender equality to be implemented. "The coming months will allow us to prepare for the leadership transition under the best possible conditions," he said.

schema.headline: Eiffel Tower chief to quit after female staff replaced by men during religious visit

title: Sir Ranulph Fiennes: Relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him
description: Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them. Speaking to BBC Ne
body: Relatives of the British explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes have said it is "very painful" he appears to have been hidden away from them. Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his former sister-in-law told the BBC that she did not know where he was, and nobody had been able to see him.It has been alleged that Sir Ranulph, 82, has been admitted to a number of care homes under assumed names, after a family rift involving his second wife, Louise Millington-Cotes.Louise Millington-Cotes did not immediately respond to the allegations, or the BBC's request for comment.Cheshire Police have said they are aware of the concerns regarding Sir Ranulph, and are satisfied he is living in an appropriate setting with suitable care.They said there were "no immediate safeguarding concerns". Sir Ranulph has not been seen in public for nearly two years, just months after opening up about a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease, a progressive disorder affecting the brain, nervous system, and muscle control.He was the first person to visit both north and south poles by surface means in the early 1980s and has been described by Guinness World Records as "the world's greatest living explorer".Spending his childhood between the UK and South Africa, he joined the British Army after leaving school, going on to serve in the SAS.Sir Ranulph's stepson, Alex Millington-Cotes, told BBC Newsnight he wanted to see the power of attorney "removed from my own mother" and placed in the hands of people who "have fully his best interests in mind"."He's not an isolated type of person, and so to see him isolated now is very painful," he said. Last week, he launched a crowdfunding campaign for legal fees to "locate and safeguard" the explorer, and so far it has raised almost £26,000. He wrote that the fundraiser had been created as "a result of our concern and desperation" after trying "multiple avenues" to locate his stepfather.Questions about Sir Ranulph's whereabouts grew in prominence after a report in the Telegraph earlier this month, external in which "members of his inner circle" raised concerns about his whereabouts. The paper also reported concerns about Sir Ranulph have been raised with the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG), the government agency which helps people to stay in control of decisions about their health and finances. In a statement to the BBC, an OPG spokesperson said: "We have a strict duty of confidentiality to all individuals who have made a lasting power of attorney, and it would be deeply inappropriate to comment on a specific case."We take all safeguarding concerns seriously and investigate thoroughly where there is the evidence and legal basis to do so."Arabella Pepper, the younger sister of Sir Ranulph's late first wife Ginny, told BBC Newsnight that she had not been able to see her former brother-in-law for over a year. "All his friends and family want to see him and take him Toblerones and cheer him up, but we don't know where is, and he's not available, he's not accessible - that's what worries us," she said.She alleges that she was only able to see him in July 2025 after she admitted herself to a care home where she had been told he was staying. "The first thing I said to him, apart from the usual greetings, was that everybody was worried about him, was looking for him, was longing to see him," Pepper told the BBC."The relief on his face was very obvious, and he said, send a message to everybody, send them my love, tell them I love them and tell them I'm longing to see them."Posting on X, BBC world affairs editor John Simpson, wrote he was "horrified to hear what's happened to my good friend Ran Fiennes"."He's the world's bravest man, and he's vulnerable. We must know what's happening to him."Starting in 1967, Sir Ranulph has been the leader of almost 20 major expeditions, according to the Explorers Club.His expedition to both the north and south poles came during the Transglobe Expedition, in which he led the first team to circumnavigate the globe from north to south.Sir Ranulph has also enjoyed a career as a prolific travel writer, as well as authoring fiction, non-fiction and biographies.

schema.headline: Sir Ranulph Fiennes: Relatives tell BBC it's 'very painful' not being able to visit him

title: Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with I'm Alive performance under Eiffel Tower
description: Celine Dion has opened Paris Fashion Week with a surprise performance of her 2002 hit I'm Alive, underneath the city's famous Eiffel Tower.The Canadia
body: Celine Dion has opened Paris Fashion Week with a surprise performance of her 2002 hit I'm Alive, underneath the city's famous Eiffel Tower.The Canadian star, who was diagnosed with a rare neurological disease called stiff person syndrome in 2022, took to the runway at the end of L'Oreal's annual show.The singer, who wore a ruched full-length velvet black gown, was later joined by famous ambassadors for the French brand, including Viola Davis, Simone Ashley, Aja Naomi King and Eva Longoria.Dion recently performed a comeback show in the city earlier this month, her first since her 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. Paris Fashion Week, showcasing women's spring/summer collections, runs until 6 October.

schema.headline: Celine Dion kicks off Paris Fashion Week with I'm Alive performance under Eiffel Tower

title: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech
description: Image source, EPA ShutterstockByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterAndy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader an
body: Image source, EPA ShutterstockByBrian WheelerPolitical reporterAndy Burnham has delivered his first speech to the Labour conference as party leader and prime minister. Here is what stood out.1. Relaxed vibes, serious contentIt was no surprise to see Andy Burnham tieless and roaming the conference stage in Liverpool, unanchored by the traditional leader's speech podium.But despite the relaxed TED talk vibe, this was sober and serious speech. He set out major new policies - not always a given on these occasions - and spoke with real emotion about his family and working class roots.There were few jokes - and in stark contrast to his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer's speech last year, he did not mention Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch once. But he also avoided mention of some of the trickier issues he faces, such as welfare reform and how his government will pay for promised increases in defence spending.2. Bringing back public controlMuch of his speech was aimed at the party faithful, with a promise to "break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path", and bring back traditional Labour values.It went down extremely well in the hall. We counted 11 standing ovations in just over an hour.The first came when he vowed to overturn Margaret Thatcher's 1980s reforms to give the public greater control over housing, water and energy.The new part was a plan to legislate later this year to repeal Thatcher's "ideological ban on public ownership of water companies".He said this would put the UK on a 10-year path to a "very different water system" - although there was not an explicit commitment to renationalisation.3. Pensions triple lock gambleThe run up to the speech was dominated by speculation about whether Burnham would scrap the state pension triple lock, which guarantees increases in line with the highest of inflation, earnings or 2.5%.In the end, it was a bit more nuanced than that.He said he would "honour" Labour's commitment to keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament.But from April 2030, the state pension would rise every year by inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, under Burnham's plans - and it will be increased in some years if needed to keep pace with average worker earnings.The change, he said, would "generate significant savings" to fund his long-held ambition of creating a National Care Service in England."I accept I may pay a political price," he told the conference. "But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off."4. Electoral reform cheered by conferenceBurnham has made no secret of his desire to scrap Westminster's first-past-the-post voting system.And his announcement of a national commission on electoral reform went down very well with many in the hall, who have been calling for it."We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard," he said to cheers.5. Emotional tribute to late fatherAs he neared the end of his speech, Burnham appeared overcome by emotion and it looked for a brief moment as though he could not carry on.He was speaking about his father Roy, who he lost to Alzheimer's earlier this month."If only, if only he had been able to appreciate that moment of the family in Downing Street," Burnham said of his first day in his new role."The son of a man who failed his 11-plus becoming prime minister."The longest ovation of all came when he pledged to "use this job to build the kind of Britain my dad wanted to see – and fight with everything I've got to keep it together".Figure caption, Watch: The big announcements in Burnham's conference speech

schema.headline: Five takeaways from Andy Burnham's Labour conference speech

title: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI
description: US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "givin
body: US President Donald Trump has ruled out any sort of joint venture with China in artificial intelligence (AI), arguing it would be tantamount to "giving away secrets" to America's main economic rival. Speaking at an event in Washington on Tuesday, Trump again argued against putting any restrictions on the technology that would stifle growth in the future, despite mounting public concern. Following Chinese President Xi Jinping's visit to the White House last week, Beijing and Washington announced the launch of a new AI dialogue, with further talks scheduled for November. The two countries also established a new communications channel to prevent misunderstandings during AI-related incidents. During Tuesday's event marking the launch of America.gov - a new AI-powered website designed to streamline government services - Trump argued the US is "leading by a lot" in the AI sector and does not want to "mix it up" with potential competitors. "If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said. "Frankly, there is nobody in third place...it's all between us and China." Trump added that while the topic of AI came up during his meeting with President Xi last week, he remains steadfast against any sort of joint cooperation to develop the technology. "Then they're going to be able to immediately gain access to things that we know that they don't know," he said, remarking that "we're leading now over China and everyone else, and I want to keep it that way". Prior to Trump's meeting with Xi, China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder AI governance.Domestically, Trump has faced increasing public concern over the potential dangers of AI and calls for additional guardrails to be put in place.A recent poll published by Politico in late September found that two of every three Americans believes there is at least a "moderate" risk that AI could destroy humanity. A significant portion of Trump supporters polled - 44% - said they would prefer if AI development could be paused. The US president, however, has repeatedly shrugged off safety concerns, referring to them as a "hoax" and comparing them to the "global warming scam" he claims is "being perpetrated by radical left Dumocrats".

schema.headline: Trump rules out joint US-China venture to develop AI

title: Nigeria's Ben Dancer dances non-stop for seven days in world record bid
description: A Nigerian dancer has completed a 168-hour dance marathon in Lagos in a bid to set a new world record.Benjamin Daniel, known as "Ben Dancer", aimed to
body: A Nigerian dancer has completed a 168-hour dance marathon in Lagos in a bid to set a new world record.Benjamin Daniel, known as "Ben Dancer", aimed to dance for seven days to break the Guinness World Records title for the longest dance marathon by an individual.Cheered on by friends and supporters at Lagos's Freedom Park, the 33-year-old reached his target time at around 03:00 local time but continued dancing for another nine hours until midday, his team says. The physically exhausted dancer has now gone to hospital for a medical check-up.Guinness World Records has confirmed to the BBC that it has received Daniel's application for the title. The current record stands at 127 hours."Benjamin's application is active and we now eagerly await submission of his evidence, which will then go through our official review and verification process before any record can be confirmed," a spokesperson for Guinness World Records said in the statement.His team said they were "elated" and emotional after watching him complete the challenge, which has been live streamed on social media.Young people gathered in recent days to cheer him on at Freedom Park in Lagos, filming his every move and dancing along from behind the barriers."It's a beautiful moment. Seeing how far he has come and witnessing him achieve this feat made me incredibly proud and grateful to God," Uche Anumudu, one of those watching, told the BBC.The current record was set by Indian dancer Srushti Sudhir Jagtap in 2023, when she was 16. Her performance focused mainly on kathak, one of India's major classical dance forms.Ben Dancer, who has been dancing professionally for 18 years and began his attempt last Tuesday, drew on Nigeria's rich dance traditions as well as its fast-changing internet culture.Afrobeats was a constant presence during his performance, alongside genres including fuji, jazz and zouk.At times, he swapped his dance clothes for traditional Nigerian outfits, including the flowing agbada and dashiki.Nigeria has more than 250 ethnic groups, with a wide range of cultural traditions.Ben Dancer's team says the performance was intended to reflect that diversity, rather than simply test his physical endurance.He underwent intensive fitness training before the attempt, changing his diet and focusing on carbohydrates and cardiovascular conditioning.During the danceathon, he ate lightly and drank fluids while taking the permitted five minutes of rest for every continuous hour of activity.He chose to dance for several hours at a time before taking an accumulated rest and a medical team was present.The scene around him became something of a street party and videos from the event went viral across social media platforms, drawing more people to the venue.Moronumubo Akodu, who repeatedly visited to support Ben Dancer throughout the week, said she was impressed by his determination but worried about the physical toll."It is actually insane, but I am so proud of him," she told the BBC.Emmanuel Ulelu, who visited the performance twice, said he noticed a striking change in the dancer's energy."On day two, you could see the stress," he said. "Even after just three hours of dancing at the location myself, I wondered how he would keep going."But when he returned 16 hours into day five, he said Ben Dancer appeared more energetic than before."It reminded me that we're capable of doing unbelievable things when how badly we want something matches and surpasses the difficulty of achieving it," he said.Nigeria has also developed a strong relationship with Guinness World Records, particularly in entertainment.In 2023, Nigerian chef Hilda Baci cooked continuously for 93 hours and 11 minutes in Lagos, which Guinness officially recognised as a new record.Her achievement sparked a surge of interest in record attempts in Nigeria, even though others have since surpassed her.Guinness says it received more than 1,500 new applications from the country within two months of her cook-a-thon, including events such as reading, singing, and crocheting."It's been brilliant to see such strong enthusiasm for record breaking across Nigeria in recent years," a Guinness spokesperson told the BBC.

schema.headline: Nigeria's Ben Dancer dances non-stop for seven days in world record bid

title: What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 13 minutes agoThe prime minister has announced plans to scrap the existing triple lock arrangement for the state pen
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 13 minutes agoThe prime minister has announced plans to scrap the existing triple lock arrangement for the state pension in order to help fund a new plan for social care. The triple lock currently guarantees that the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is the highest.Andy Burnham said he would honour the pledge given in Labour's 2024 manifesto to keep the triple lock unchanged in the current Parliament.However, the PM said that from April 2030 the arrangement will change, with the state pension rising every year at least by inflation or 2.5%.The link to rises in yearly average earnings, which is the factor currently setting the rise under the triple lock, will be gone on an annual basis and instead be reflected over time.What is the state pension and how much is it?The state pension is a payment made every four weeks by the government, to people who have reached the qualifying age and have paid enough National Insurance (NI) contributions.Since 6 April 2026: the new flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 is £241.30 a week, or £12,547.60 a yearthe old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 is £184.90 a week, or £9,614.80 a yearMany people on the old basic state pension may also receive the additional state pension, external. In general, you need 35 years of qualifying contributions to get a full state pension.Some people may have gaps in their NI record if, for example, they have lived abroad or taken time off to care for children.It is possible to make voluntary payments to boost your contribution history. Since April 2025, you have only been able to make payments for the previous six years. Data suggested that the state pension will increase in April 2027, meaning:the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on nowthe old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on nowThe government will confirm the rise, possibly in October's Budget.How does the state pension 'triple lock' work?Under the triple lock system, the state pension increases each April in line with whichever of three measures is the highest:inflation in the September of the previous year, using a measure called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI)the average increase in total wages, including bonuses, across the UK for May to July of the previous yearor 2.5%The rise in wages of 3.9% is likely to determine the April 2027 state pension increase.The triple lock was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010.It was designed to ensure the value of the state pension wasn't overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.The Labour government has previously said it would keep the triple lock until the end of the current Parliament.But since that commitment, there has been intense debate over the cost of the triple lock and whether it is justified.In July 2025, the government's official forecaster said the cost of the triple lock guarantee was set to be three times higher by the end of the decade than was originally anticipated when it began. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said the annual cost is set to reach £15.5bn by 2030.It said the cost of the state pension has risen steadily over the past eight decades, and now equates to £138bn, or around half the total amount the government spent on benefits.In July, the influential Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think-tank suggested that the triple lock should be scrapped as part of a wider pensions overhaul.What has Andy Burnham said about the future of the triple lock?At his speech to the Labour Party conference, Burnham announced a plan to end the existing triple lock from 2030, which would see the annual link to earnings growth removed."The state pension will continue to rise every year at least by prices or 2.5%," he said."And it will hold its value relative to earnings over time so that pensioners will always share in the rising prosperity of the nation."But this change will generate significant savings which we will use to build up our national care service."The IFS called the proposed change a "great improvement", saying Burnham had "neutered the worst element of the triple lock"."State pensions will still rise, but more sustainably," said Jonathan Cribb, deputy director at the IFS.However, he warned that "we should not expect this reform to save enough that it could fund universal social care in the next parliament".Will state pensioners pay income tax?The expected increase in April 2027 would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and so liable to pay about £91 next year in income tax.The Labour government – when Rachel Reeves was chancellor – pledged that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay.In his speech to the Labour Party conference, Burnham reiterated that low-income pensioners would not have to pay income tax in this Parliament.The majority of pensioners are already income taxpayers owing to the addition of other pension income, on top of the state pension.What is the state pension age and how is it changing?Almost 13 million people currently receive the state pension.Men and women born between 6 October 1954 and 5 April1960 start receiving their pension at the age of 66.But for people born after this date, the state pension age is increasing in two phases:a gradual rise to 67 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1960a gradual rise to 68 between 2044 and 2046 for those born on, or after, 5 April 1977The rise from 66 to 67 began in April 2026. The first affected are those born between 6 April and 5 May 1960, who will have to wait an extra month. The increase is expected to save the Treasury about £10bn a year by 2030. But charities have warned that it will disproportionately affect areas of the UK where life expectancy is lower, and those on lower incomes.A government review is considering whether to delay the second phase, which would currently take the state pension age to 68 between 2044 and 2046. What is pension credit and how much is it worth?Depending on their overall income, those above retirement age may also be entitled to pension credit, external in addition to the basic state pension. Pension credit increased by 4.8% in April 2026.If your income is above the stated limits, you may still be eligible for pension credit if you have a disability or care for someone.Anyone who qualifies for pension credit may also be entitled to other financial support, including housing benefit, a reduction in council tax, help with heating costs and the warm home discount scheme.

schema.headline: What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?

title: LPU Phagwara: A rape rumour sends an Indian university into turmoil and empties hostels
description: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostelsImage source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some violent protesters a
body: How an alleged rape sent an Indian university into turmoil and emptied hostelsImage source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Some violent protesters allegedly torched police cars parked on the highway on Sunday ByZoya Mateen & Azadeh MoshiriBBC News, DelhiOne of India's largest private universities has suspended classes after an unverified allegation that a female student was raped on campus set off protests that descended into violence.Police say they have registered a case and are trying to verify whether last week's alleged rape at Lovely Professional University (LPU) did happen. The university has categorically denied the allegation.Police say no student has come forward to say she was assaulted, investigators have yet to identify the alleged victim or the perpetrator, and CCTV footage examined so far has yielded no evidence of an attack.But rumours on student WhatsApp groups led to unrest over the weekend at the sprawling 600-acre university in Punjab that draws students from India and abroad.Founded in 2005 by a family whose business began with a small sweet shop, LPU has grown into a largely self-contained world of hostels and lecture halls, with thousands of young people living on campus.Images and videos showed vehicles in flames, crowds filling a major highway and police wielding canes as unrest spilled beyond the university gates. Police vehicles were damaged, officers injured and parts of the campus was vandalised.By Monday, the highway had reopened and the campus was calmer, but heavily policed.University authorities described the claims circulating on social media as false and baseless, but it did little to reassure students with hostels emptying within hours. Key exams were postponed and students were allowed to go home.Following demands from protesting students, police registered a rape case against "an unidentified person" and formed a seven-member special investigation team, or SIT, to investigate.Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Lovely Professional University has suspended classes for 10 days amid violent protests What happened?The unrest began in the early hours of 27 September, when word spread that a female student had been raped in or near one of the university's hostels a few days earlier.The suspect was variously described - by students and in media reports - as a plumber, painter or construction worker. Some students said the assault had occurred on 23 September and accused the university of failing to act after being informed.BBC Punjabi found that messages about the allegation had circulated through WhatsApp groups. As they travelled, crowds gathered.Hundreds eventually spilled on to National Highway 44, a major route between Delhi and Punjab, blocking traffic for more than 15 hours. By Sunday evening, university property had been damaged, objects set alight and stones thrown at police vehicles. Videos showed police striking protesters with canes, although police later denied carrying out a baton-charge.Behind the gates, students described a night of fear."We were sitting with knives and scissors," Arya, a student, told BBC Punjabi. Students had been told to lock themselves inside their rooms, she said, while people knocked on their doors. "We were just thinking that somehow this night would pass and we would get out of here."Police later arrived and made them feel safer, she said. By the next day, she wanted to leave. "Our parents also want us to just get out of here."Image source, BBC PunjabiImage caption, Arya, a student at the college, says they thought about nothing but leaving the campus on the night of violence So why have police lodged a case?That the police open a case and investigate the allegation was among the protesters' central demands."The students have been demanding that an FIR  [First Information Report] is to be registered, but the students could not provide us with any victim's name," senior police official Naveen Singla told the BBC.Police nevertheless registered an FIR under India's rape law against an unidentified person. An FIR formally records an allegation for investigation; it does not establish that a crime occurred.Singla said investigators had also begun examining CCTV footage. The preliminary search, he told the BBC, had so far shown no outsider entering a room."As of now, it can't be verified that rape has happened or not," he said.But they are continuing to examine the footage."The campus is quite large, so we haven't been able to see all the cameras yet," Sinha told reporters on Monday. "We have initially checked the places that the students had mentioned, but we will get to the bottom of this."Image source, Pardeep Sharma/BBCImage caption, Protesting students had earlier blocked a nearby highway which was opened later on Monday Why did the protests grow so large?It is difficult to say. What began with an allegation of rape quickly became a broader protest over security, the university's response and, eventually, the violence itself.There was also growing uncertainty over who was on the campus. Some students insisted the demonstrations had begun peacefully and blamed outsiders for at least some of the violence. Others told BBC Punjabi of seeing masked or unfamiliar people inside the university."We were really scared," said Pawan, a student. "It became a complete battlefield."Another student, Aniket Singh, said outsiders had entered a women's hostel and knocked on doors claiming to be police officers. Police have since confirmed that outsiders were among the crowds, but said they were still trying to establish who they were and what role they played.Amid that confusion, the university's attempt to dispel the rape allegation produced a controversy of its own.On Monday, LPU released a video of three women living in the hostel room that had been linked to the alleged assault. They said nothing had happened there and asked people to stop disturbing them.The same students later alleged in another video that university officials had instructed them what to say, edited the recording and posted it without their consent. Those claims have not been independently verified. LPU has not commented on the students' allegations.Another claim circulating during the protests sought to connect the alleged rape with the recent suicide of a female LPU student from Telangana state. Police say investigations into her death had already begun and there is no verified evidence linking the two cases.Image source, ANIImage caption, There is heavy police presence around the university campus since the unrest What is happening now?For now, life on campus has been interrupted. Regular classes have been suspended for 10 days and exams postponed. Students have been asked to return home after consulting their parents or guardians.Those who are staying have been advised to stay in their residences and avoid further unrest.The Punjab State Women's Commission has also sought the FIR, details of the investigation and information about arrangements for students' safety.The investigation now has two separate questions to answer: whether there is evidence of the assault that set the protests in motion? And who was responsible for the violence that followed?Addressing the students on Monday, LPU's pro-chancellor Rashmi Mittal said she was hurt that despite the university's many channels for students to raise concerns, they had instead "believed the rumour that was spreading". She also alleged that outsiders had joined the unrest."I feel students can't do this," she said.Additional reporting by Harmandeep Singh, BBC PunjabiFollow BBC News India on Instagram, external, YouTube,, external X, external and Facebook, external.

schema.headline: LPU Phagwara: A rape rumour sends an Indian university into turmoil and empties hostels

title: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift dominates but do music videos matter?
description: Taylor Swift dominated the VMAs, but do music videos still matter? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor Swift became the most successful ar
body: Taylor Swift dominated the VMAs, but do music videos still matter? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Taylor Swift became the most successful artist in the history of the VMAs on SundayByNaomi Clarke and Andrew RogersBBC NewsbeatWe're far from the days of blockbuster music videos playing back-to-back on TV channels like MTV.Catchy hooks and sleek dance routines now dominate social media feeds, each hoping to stop people in their tracks long enough for them to give a new song a chance.  The evolution of this landscape was cemented last year when MTV axed five music channels in the UK after almost 40 years of rolling footage. But despite the broadcaster reacting to the changes in viewing habits, its Video Music Awards (VMAs) still appear to hold power over music A-listers.Pop music heavyweights, including Taylor Swift, Madonna and Charli XCX, were among those who turned up on Sunday to accept prizes and deliver dramatic performances. Cinematographer Melissa Cofie tells BBC Newsbeat that while these award shows "may seem very performative to others", they are "so important" to those in the music industry."The sleepless nights, the months, the weeks that it takes to put together a music video, it's almost as much work as you would put into a film itself," she says. But do music videos still hold the same importance for fans as they once did?Image source, TAS Rights ManagementImage caption, Graham Norton and Domhnall Gleeson were among the stars who featured in Taylor Swift's Opalite videoCofie, who has directed music videos, feels their purpose has evolved over the last couple of decades.For her, they're more of a way to "connect with artists" and for them to express their vision, rather than a crucial part of their press run like they were in the 2000s. Pop stars like Swift, Sabrina Carpenter and Olivia Rodrigo are among those who still lean on videos heavily to build out the visual world for each of their albums' eras.Swift, who broke the record for most MTV VMA wins ever last weekend, is known for big budget productions which fans trawl through for Easter eggs - clues that could point to something else she has planned.She also often enlists the help of her star-studded contact book, with her recent video for Opalite jam-packed with famous faces, including Graham Norton, Lewis Capaldi, Cillian Murphy, Domhnall Gleeson and Jodie Turner-Smith.However, the music video was released exclusively on Spotify and Apple Music in February, and did not appear on YouTube until 48 hours later.Industry analysts speculated at the time that the exclusivity period was due to a change in the US chart rules, where songs streamed on YouTube will no longer count towards the Top 100.This change came into place in January, with YouTube saying it was ending its decade-long partnership with Billboard, external as it claimed the chart uses an "outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported"."This doesn't reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don't have a subscription," it added.And while most artists don't have Swift-level budgets to start with, this change may have further discouraged US artists' to throw a lot of money into creating elaborate music videos.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, K-Pop superstars like BTS often release multiple music videos for one song However, in international markets like the world of K-Pop, creating visually aesthetic music videos featuring polished choreography has become essential when promoting the act to a global audience.The genre's superstars like BTS and Blackpink often also release dance practice videos and behind-the-scenes clips alongside traditional music videos. These variations offer them more content to clip up for social media, and also helps drive up their streaming numbers and global chart positions. Cofie feels the rise of platforms like TikTok, Instagram and YouTube has "100%" changed the way videos are consumed and therefore, how they are created. But she doesn't see this as a "blow" to the industry and isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly"."It kind of pushes us to think: 'Okay, how can each scene, each still be the one that captures people's attention?'," she says. "We don't have five minutes anymore. We've actually got two minutes, sometimes less."I think it pushes us as creatives to think how can we get the point across quickly in the best way possible."Image source, Anastasia A. ArsentyevaImage caption, Cinematographer Melissa Cofie isn't "discouraged that things are changing so quickly"Gener8ion and Swedish rapper Yung Lean's cinematic music video for their collaboration track Storm is a testament to how a short mesmerising visual moment can make a song go viral online. The scene from within the full video sees Lean, acting as a teenage bully, stand amongst a group of dancers who are also dressed in school uniforms as they perform hypnotic, synchronised choreography, external.They recreated the routine at the VMAs, and while it lost out on the coveted video of the year award to Swift's The Fate of Ophelia, clips of the performance once again have flooded social media.Cofie admits it has been "really tough" to come up with "new creative ideas" like this since short clips have boomed post-pandemic, but says she is continually inspired by new music videos. And her advice to artists and crews who still want to create music videos? "It's cliche, but just to continue being creative and just exploring every corner of your mind, any idea that you have, just do it," she says."Don't worry that it's already been done and it's not original because each and every person's interpretation or perspective is different."  Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: MTV VMAs: Taylor Swift dominates but do music videos matter?

title: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat
description: Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-
body: Spain's coalition government has approved new housing measures following protests over the country's housing crisis, sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last week.Ministers met on Tuesday to discuss the proposals, which include a ban on evictions until 2030.Announcing the measures, Health Minister Mónica García said they would bring relief to more than five million people - but opposition politician Míriam Nogueras said the agreement left "small landlords out in the cold".The proposals - which have been presented in the form of two decrees - come into effect immediately, but must be approved by Congress within a month, although the government hopes to hold the vote as soon as this Friday. Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government lacks a majority in parliament and has struggled to get right-leaning parties to approve previous decrees.In April, a decree seeking to roll over rental contracts was blocked by right-leaning parties.García, of the Sumar alliance, said other measures agreed upon on Tuesday included the rolling over of contracts until 2028; stricter regulation of short-term and room rentals; and banning the purchase of housing by investment firms."It is time to intervene in the speculative housing market and start striking a balance between ordinary citizens and vulture funds," García said.Referencing the protests, she added: "Thanks to the mobilisations and the encampments. Without you, this would not have been possible."But Nogueras, spokeswoman for the centre-right Catalan nationalists of Junts party, said: "We all agreed that evictions - where the property is owned by a fund, a vulture fund, run by someone managing millions of euros - obviously need to be stopped."Lumping together in this category those who have invested their savings in a flat, a restaurant or a property - putting them all in the same basket - is a mistake," she told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE.The minority government, which is made up of the Sánchez's ruling Socialists and junior partner the Sumar alliance, has 30 days from the decrees' publication to reach an agreement in parliament. Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez urged political parties to support the decrees after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal last week."Congress has the opportunity to tell Maricarmen that her suffering was worth it... and that many people will benefit from her battle", she said.But Valeria Racu, a spokeswoman for the Madrid Tenants' Union, said the battle had "only just begun", and called for more protests across Spain next weekend."We all have our eyes on the text, on the small print, to make sure this is the Maricarmen decree," added Alicia del Río, another spokeswoman for the organisation.The two decrees approved by the cabinet contain enough to at least suggest that the government has been listening carefully to the demands of the activists who have been protesting in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere in recent days. The temporary ban on evictions, the rolling over of rental contracts and the ban on investment firms - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property are all the kinds of policies that have been discussed by housing activists in recent days.Pablo Bustinduy, minister of social rights, described the measures approved by the cabinet as "a first step towards the economic and social transformation of the country".Bustinduy and his Sumar alliance had entered the negotiations with Sánchez's Socialists determined to take a stand on this issue, which is one they feel strongly about. Sumar's tough stance was a major reason why talks between the coalition partners on the decrees went down to the wire ahead of Tuesday's cabinet meeting.While the relatively bold new measures may please many on the left, they have raised the hackles of the Junts, whose support is again likely to be needed to approve them. Junts and other parties on the right tend to be reluctant to intervene in the housing market, particularly if it means tipping the balance of the law in favour of tenants and against landlords, many of who are their natural electorate.The question now is whether the social momentum generated by the Maricarmen Abascal case will override such reservations and manage to ensure this package of measures becomes law.Ahead of the government's announcement on Tuesday, the lawyer for Abascal, who has become a symbol of Spain's housing crisis, said she would be allowed to return to her home after reaching a deal with the company that owns it on Monday.Abascal, who was admitted to hospital after being forcibly removed from the apartment on a stretcher, was unable to attend the meeting and is yet to sign the deal.Abascal's father first rented the flat in 1956 and she had continued to live in it after her parents died, with a cap on the rent, until investment company Urbagestión bought the property in 2018. It raised the monthly rent to more than her monthly pension, leaving her unable to pay it.Abascal's case is not unique.In the north-eastern city of Zaragoza, another woman's eviction was temporarily suspended on Tuesday, the European Pressphoto Agency reported. Esmeralda Tejero, 51, has lived in a flat in the city for eight years with her 11-year-old daughter, but stopped paying her rent some time ago as she could not afford it on top of her daily living costs, she told Catalan newspaper el Periódico on Monday.Protests calling for housing relief measures broke out last week in Madrid and have spread to other cities including Barcelona, Seville, Malaga and Cadiz.Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday demanding stronger protection for tenants in the face of a housing shortage and soaring rents.Hundreds of tents have been set up in the famous public square of Puerta del Sol since.

schema.headline: Spain announces ban on evictions after protests over 87-year-old woman's removal from flat

title: 'Ship buster' missiles sink old US warship in live fire training off Scotland
description: Figure caption, The decommissioned USS Klakring was sunk at the Ministry of Defence's Hebrides rangeUpdated 7 hours agoA decommissioned American warsh
body: Figure caption, The decommissioned USS Klakring was sunk at the Ministry of Defence's Hebrides rangeUpdated 7 hours agoA decommissioned American warship has been sunk off Scotland's west coast during a training exercise involving both US forces and the Royal Navy. USS Klakring was hit by missiles and a torpedo before sinking in the North Atlantic about 170 miles (274km) off the Outer Hebrides last Monday.The US Navy said the ship went a through "rigorous" cleaning process first, and personnel checked for the presence of whales and dolphins before the live-firing exercise started.Other warships, including an aircraft carrier in 2006, have been deliberately sunk at sea by the US as part of training and to create artificial reefs for marine life.Image source, US Naval Forces Europe-AfricaImage caption, A 43-year-old frigate was used for target practiceThe former guided missile frigate was struck by a missile from USS Paul Ignatius and a torpedo from USS Massachusetts as part of Exercise Atlantic Thunder 2026.The UK's Royal Navy also tested "ship-busting" weapons during the exercise.HMS Portland, a Type 23 frigate, fired a Naval Sea Missile (NSM) - an advanced sea skimming weapon that can travel close to supersonic speeds and hit a target more than100 miles away. The ship's Wildcat helicopter also fired Sea Venom missiles at the target. The Royal Navy said it was the first live firing of the weapons from a Wildcat helicopter at a realistic target.USS Klakring entered service in 1983 and was decommissioned in 2013.It was named after Rear Adm Thomas B Klakring, who was awarded three US Navy Crosses as the commander of a submarine during World War Two.Image source, US Naval Forces Europe-AfricaImage caption, USS Klakring was hit by a missile and torpedo during Exercise Atlantic ThunderThe US Navy said sinking exercises were prepared in strict compliance with environmental regulations.A spokesperson said: "The extensive preparations for the exercise include putting the hulk through a rigorous cleaning process to remove contaminants and old equipment, thereby assuring that the environmental impact of the exercise is minimal. "Sinking ex-navy vessels, which are specially prepared as targets, provides a practicable method for conducting large scale exercises of this type, to train at the high level required by the armed forces."

schema.headline: 'Ship buster' missiles sink old US warship in live fire training off Scotland

title: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage in Channel
description: Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcast
body: Thomas is alleged to have used his social media platform to livestream himself from the English Channel at around 16:30 BST on 22 September, broadcasting to a large audience, the court heard.He is accused of slashing a boat that had been used by migrants, which was adrift in the sea, while a rescue crew member was on board.He is also alleged to have said "this is what needs to happen" and "this is England, this isn't France any more".Simon Pentol KC, defending, had proposed a "package of bail conditions" as an alternative to Thomas being remanded in custody and described the allegation against his client as "politically charged and fundamentally flawed".On his decision to refuse bail, the Judge James Newton-Price KC, said: "I am not concerned with the political issues or motivations in this matter and I put them aside in deciding this matter."A handful of supporters waited outside the court to hear the outcome of the hearing.

schema.headline: Daniel Thomas refused bail over alleged boat damage in Channel

title: Manchester City charges: Premier League confirms club guilty of all charges related to financial rule breaches
description: Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of its commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m,
body: Manchester City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of its commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m, the Premier League says.The League confirmed that City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.An independent commission found that, during that time period, the club arranged the "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs".The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.News broke last week that City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching, but on Tuesday the Premier League published a redacted version of the commission's report.The commission's report said the charges "concerned well over 100 alleged individual breaches of Premier League Rules across four broad charge categories". It also found the club guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.The sham commercial deals were described as being part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830.69m. "The relevant sponsorship agreements were found to be shams, or at minimum did not reflect their economic substance," the commission said. It also describes "deliberate or reckless conduct intended to circumvent the Premier League rules" and that the "sham" scheme devised by City allowed the club "to avoid recording what would otherwise have been the largest single-season loss in Premier League history in 2009-10".Richard Masters, chief executive of the Premier League, said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently."It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously."The Premier League also said that City's sanction "will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission". The League's rules state that the hearing must remain private and confidential, and that the club has the right to appeal the commission's findings. City have until Friday 2 October to submit their appeal.Lisa Nandy MP, the Culture, Media & Sport secretary, told the BBC: "It's incredibly serious, the Premier League report is incredibly stark."This is causing a lot of concern for Man City fans and all fans of Premier League football."

schema.headline: Manchester City charges: Premier League confirms club guilty of all charges related to financial rule breaches

title: Nowak killer Vickrum Digwa given leave to appeal against sentence
description: After stabbing Nowak, who came from Chafford Hundred in Essex, Digwa lied to police that he was the victim of a racist attack.The case later sparked p
body: After stabbing Nowak, who came from Chafford Hundred in Essex, Digwa lied to police that he was the victim of a racist attack.The case later sparked protests after police body-worn footage was released showing officers failing to give Nowak first aid and instead handcuffing him as he lay dying, despite him telling officers he could not breathe.The Independent Office for Police Conduct previously said it was investigating two officers for potential gross misconduct.Twelve police officers and a police dog were injured during the protests in Southampton on 2 June.Demonstrators gathered outside the city centre police station before moving to an area near the Digwa family home and the murder scene.More than 30 people have so far been charged with violent disorder following the incident.On 15 June, former Solicitor General Ellie Reeves KC referred the case to the Court of Appeal under the Unduly Lenient Sentence scheme.Sikh leaders have reported a "backlash" and increase in "hate crime" against their community following the case.

schema.headline: Nowak killer Vickrum Digwa given leave to appeal against sentence

title: Wayne Rooney says Manchester United do not deserve Manchester City titles
description: Wayne Rooney says his former club Manchester United do not deserve to be awarded Premier League titles if rivals Manchester City are stripped of them
body: Wayne Rooney says his former club Manchester United do not deserve to be awarded Premier League titles if rivals Manchester City are stripped of them for breaching financial rules.City have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.The financial charges relate to the period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, while they were also accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 to February 2023.Sanctions are yet to be announced and City plan to appeal against the decision.One possible punishment could be the club being stripped of top-flight titles. They have won the Premier League eight times since Sheikh Mansour's takeover in 2009, three of which were in the period when they were accused of breaking financial rules.Rooney was part of the United side that finished runners-up to City in 2011-2012 but does not want to be awarded the title retrospectively. Speaking on the Stick to United podcast,, external he said: "I wouldn't feel comfortable about accepting another Premier League medal if I'm being honest, because I don't think we deserve it. We didn't do enough that season to win the league."I'm thinking as their players, they're there doing everything they can to win the Premier League title and in their minds they've done it."And, if those players have got no understanding of what's going on above them, then if that happened to me - if all of a sudden Manchester United have been doing the same and I'm getting my Premier League medals taken away from me - I'd be absolutely devastated."They might take them away but I wouldn't want it because I don't feel as a team we deserved it that year because we obviously didn't finish first."Rooney's former United team-mates Rio Ferdinand and David de Gea both posted on social media after news of the guilty verdict emerged on Friday, suggesting they should be awarded retrospective title wins.And former Stoke City boss Tony Pulis said he felt "cheated" after his side were beaten by the Blues in the 2011 FA Cup final. "When I've heard of ex-team-mates and people saying, 'we've won another medal', I'm happy with the five I've won," said Rooney."I wouldn't want this one just sat there... 15 years later or whatever it was you get a medal because City cheated. I wouldn't feel comfortable."The question is, would I want to receive that medal for finishing second? No."Some players might. I just wouldn't feel comfortable for accepting a Premier League medal for finishing second."While Rooney is against titles being taken away from City, he does believe they should be relegated."I do think we're going to see City getting relegated," said the 40-year-old. "However that happens I don't know but I think we're going to see them get relegated."Rooney added: "I'd put them in the lowest league they can go in and then put restrictions on them in terms of how much money they can spend for the next three or four seasons."If you're just putting them in the Championship, and I get that's a massive punishment, they're going to come back up. Where, I feel if they have got restrictions... League Two, whatever... that could be very difficult for them."For instance, if they got a 20-point deduction for the next three years then players won't want to stay there. If it's Championship for a season, you could talk players round. "I'd go as big as I can really."Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino, meanwhile, says "we have lived through a period of deception".Pochettino managed three clubs in the Premier League during the period covering City's charges, with the 54-year-old spending 15 months at Southampton, five years at Tottenham and a single season with Chelsea. "Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," said Pochettino. "It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't. "Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] - what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard."It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened. "We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception."Earlier this month, Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-17 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches and that it should be "awarded" to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up. Sources have told BBC Sport that other top flight clubs are seeking legal advice over possible compensation claims following the decision against City. City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.The club were referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks."Where were the controls?" said Pochettino on City being found guilty. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls?"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months. "I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer]."Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]? "They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange."On Tuesday, La Liga president Javier Tebas said he agreed with Pochettino and believes City should face the most severe sanctions possible after an "era of disappointment"."In my opinion, the most severe sanction provided for under the Premier League regulations should be applied," Tebas, 64, told BBC Sport at a summit in London hosted by global players' union Fifapro."Given the number of years involved, the repeated breaches, the denial and the lack of cooperation, the most severe sanction allowed under the Premier League rules is what should be imposed, although I do not know exactly what that sanction would be."On Tuesday, La Liga president Javier Tebas said he agreed with Pochettino's verdict and added: "In my opinion, the most severe sanction provided for under the Premier League regulations should be applied."Given the number of years involved, the repeated breaches, the denial and the lack of co-operation, the most severe sanction allowed under the Premier League rules is what should be imposed, although I do not know exactly what that sanction would be," Tebas, 64, told BBC Sport at a summit in London hosted by global players' union Fifapro.The Spaniard added that he had been raising concerns about City's conduct for "many years".

schema.headline: Wayne Rooney says Manchester United do not deserve Manchester City titles
